passages.t: A man and his father's wife, and ‘hand this man over to Satan’
passages.happening:
Paul turns to a report that shocked him. “It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is intolerable even among pagans: A man has his father’s wife” (verse 1).

What troubles Paul most is the church's response. “And you are proud! Shouldn’t you rather have been stricken with grief and have removed from your fellowship the man who did this?” (verse 2).

Paul says he has already reached a judgment, though he is far away. He is present with them “in spirit” (verse 3). When they gather in the name of the Lord Jesus, with the power of the Lord Jesus, they are to act (verse 4).

He tells them to “hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
‘His father's wife’ almost certainly means the man's stepmother. Paul does not say ‘his mother’. She may have been widowed or divorced from the man's father. The man was living with her, as a partner or as a wife. The law of Moses forbade it, and Paul says even the pagans of Corinth would not accept it.

Paul says nothing to the woman. Many readers take that to mean she was not a member of the church. His words are for the man, and above all for the church.

Why did the church do nothing? Paul does not say. Some readers think the man was a person of wealth and standing whom few would dare to challenge, in a city where patrons were honoured. Others think some believers had decided that, with their new freedom in Christ, what they did with their bodies no longer mattered. Paul will answer that idea in chapter 6. Either way the church was ‘proud’, the word Paul uses for being puffed up. They may even have thought their tolerance was a sign of how free and spiritual they were.

Notice that Paul does not act alone. The church is to act ‘when you are assembled’. The decision belongs to the gathered church, under the name and power of Jesus, not to one leader.

‘Satan’ is a Hebrew word meaning the accuser or the adversary. In the Bible he is the enemy of God and of God's people.
passages.ot:
The law of Moses forbade this very union. “You must not have sexual relations with your father’s wife; it would dishonor your father” (Leviticus 18:8). Deuteronomy says it again: “A man is not to marry his father’s wife, so that he will not dishonor his father’s marriage bed” (Deuteronomy 22:30).

Those laws come in a chapter that sets Israel apart from the nations around it: “Do not defile yourselves by any of these practices” (Leviticus 18:24). Paul's point is sharper still. The church was tolerating what even the nations around it would not.

Israel's community also had to deal with grave sin among its own people. The law's repeated words, “So you must purge the evil from among you” (Deuteronomy 17:7), stand behind Paul's command at the end of the chapter.
passages.hard:
What does ‘hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh’ mean?

The phrase is hard, and it should not be made to sound easy. Most readers today take it to mean that the church should put the man out of its fellowship. The church is the place where Christ is honoured as Lord. Outside it lies the world, which Paul sees as the realm where Satan has power. To ‘hand over to Satan’ is to send the man out of the church's shared life and protection, back into that world. On this reading ‘the flesh’ means the man's sinful self, as it often does in Paul. The hope is that, cut off from the fellowship, he will come to his senses and turn back. Others take ‘the flesh’ more bodily, and think Paul expected the man to suffer in body as well, much as 11:30 speaks of sickness in the church. On both readings the purpose is plain in the verse itself: ‘so that his spirit may be saved’. The aim is rescue, not destruction of the person.

Paul uses the same words once more, of two men he ‘handed over to Satan to be taught not to blaspheme’ (1 Timothy 1:20). There too the aim is that they learn. And many readers think 2 Corinthians shows what such discipline should lead to: “So instead, you ought to forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow” (2 Corinthians 2:7). Whether that is the same man is not certain. The spirit of it is clear.

How should churches practise discipline? Churches have answered in different ways. Some can keep a person from Communion for a time, hoping to bring them back. Some practise church discipline carried out by elders, and some by the whole congregation. Others use little formal discipline and rely on pastoral care. All take their lead from passages such as this one and Matthew 18:15-17. These notes do not choose among the churches' practices.

This passage has also been badly misused, and that must be faced. Church discipline must never be used to silence someone who has been harmed, to protect someone who has done harm, or to punish someone for asking questions or telling the truth. Paul's whole concern here is that a church protected a wrongdoer by doing nothing. Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities, whom Paul calls “God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4). A church meeting is never a substitute for that.

A word to anyone who has been hurt by a church's discipline, or shunned by a church or a family. What happened to you may have been wrong, and it is not wrong to grieve it. Paul's goal was always restoration and comfort, never cruelty or contempt. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). If this still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul says the church was proud when it should have grieved. Ask whether you have ever been proud of being tolerant about something that was harming a person. Then ask the opposite question: have you been quick to condemn others, and slow to seek their good? Paul's aim, even in his hardest words, is that the person be saved.

passages.t: The old leaven, and ‘Christ, our Passover lamb’
passages.happening:
“Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough?” (verse 6).

“Get rid of the old leaven, that you may be a new unleavened batch, as you really are. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (verse 7).

“Therefore let us keep the feast, not with the old bread, leavened with malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Leaven was not the yeast sold in packets today. It was a lump of old, fermented dough kept back from the last baking and worked into the new batch to make it rise. A little of it spread through the whole lump. So leaven was a good picture of how something small spreads.

At Passover, Jewish households searched their homes and cleared out every bit of leaven. For seven days they ate bread made without it. The feast remembered the night God brought Israel out of Egypt in haste.

Paul's Gentile hearers may not have kept Passover, but they had heard the Scriptures read, and Paul expects them to follow the picture. The ‘old leaven’ is the old life, and here especially the sin the church has let stay among them. Left alone, it will spread.

Notice the order in verse 7. ‘That you may be a new unleavened batch, as you really are.’ Paul does not say: clean yourselves up so that you may become God's people. He says: you already are a new batch, because Christ has been sacrificed. Now live like it. What God has done comes first. What they must do follows.

‘Sincerity’ means being without mixture: pure all the way through, with nothing hidden.
passages.ot:
The whole picture comes from Exodus 12. On the night Israel left Egypt each household killed a lamb and marked its doorframes with the blood. God said, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13). Then came the feast of Unleavened Bread: “For seven days you must eat unleavened bread. On the first day you are to remove the leaven from your houses” (Exodus 12:15).

Paul says Christ is that lamb. All four Gospels place Jesus's death at the time of Passover. John the Baptist called him “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), and Peter speaks of “the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19). As the lamb's blood marked Israel's rescue, Christ's death marks the rescue of a new people.

Jesus himself used leaven as a picture of something that spreads, for good, “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven” (Matthew 13:33), and for harm: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod” (Mark 8:15).
passages.asks: Paul says believers already are a new batch because of what Christ has done. Ask whether you live from that, or whether you are still trying to earn it. Then ask what ‘old leaven’ you have let stay, a resentment, a habit, a quiet dishonesty, that is spreading further than you think.

passages.t: Not the world, but the church: ‘God will judge those outside’
passages.happening:
Paul clears up a misunderstanding. “I wrote you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people” (verse 9).

But he did not mean the people of the world, the immoral, the greedy, swindlers or idolaters. “In that case you would have to leave this world” (verse 10).

What he meant was this: “not to associate with anyone who claims to be a brother but is sexually immoral or greedy, an idolater or a verbal abuser, a drunkard or a swindler. With such a man do not even eat” (verse 11).

“What business of mine is it to judge those outside the church? Are you not to judge those inside? God will judge those outside” (verses 12-13).

He ends with the words of Scripture: “Expel the wicked man from among you” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Paul had written to Corinth before, and that letter is lost (verse 9). The Corinthians seem to have taken it to mean they should keep away from every immoral person in the city. In a busy Roman port, where business, family and friendship all meant meeting people of every kind, that was impossible. Perhaps some used it as an excuse to do nothing at all.

Paul says they have it backwards. Believers are not to cut themselves off from the world. They are to live in it, eat with their neighbours, trade with them and be their friends. The church is not sent to police the world. ‘God will judge those outside.’

What the church must deal with is its own life. A person who ‘claims to be a brother’, who belongs to the church and calls himself a believer, and yet goes on openly in serious sin, cannot be treated as if nothing were wrong.

Notice the list. It is not only about sex. Greed, idolatry, abusive speech, drunkenness and cheating are all on it. A church that is strict about one of these and easy on greed or cruel words has not listened to Paul.

‘Do not even eat’ matters in that world. Eating together was a sign of friendship and acceptance. For the church it included the shared meal at which they kept the Lord's Supper. Paul means: do not carry on as if this person's life were fine. He does not mean: treat him as an enemy. Paul says elsewhere, “Yet do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother” (2 Thessalonians 3:15).
passages.ot:
The words ‘Expel the wicked man from among you’ come from a refrain in Deuteronomy. In the Berean Standard Bible it reads, “So you must purge the evil from among you” (Deuteronomy 17:7). It is repeated after several laws (Deuteronomy 13:5; 19:19; 22:21; 24:7). Israel was to deal with grave sin inside its own community so that it would not spread.

Paul takes the words and changes what they lead to. In Deuteronomy the laws that end with this refrain often carried the death penalty. For the church, the most it may do is put a person outside its fellowship, with the hope of bringing him back.

The teaching of Jesus stands behind ‘not the world’. Jesus prayed for his followers, “I am not asking that You take them out of the world, but that You keep them from the evil one” (John 17:15). He himself ate with tax collectors and sinners, and said, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick” (Matthew 9:12).
passages.hard:
Does this passage tell Christians to condemn the people around them? No. It says the opposite. ‘What business of mine is it to judge those outside the church?’ Paul does not send the church to police the city, to shun its neighbours, or to demand that people who do not share its faith live by its rules. ‘God will judge those outside.’ Churches have often reversed Paul's order, hard on the world and soft on themselves. Paul asks for the reverse.

Nor does ‘do not even eat’ give anyone leave for cruelty. The person is still a brother, to be warned and won back. And this passage, like the one above, must never be turned against someone who has been harmed, or used to shut out a person who asks honest questions.
passages.asks: Paul tells the church to be open to the world and honest with itself. Ask which way round you have it. Are there people outside the church you hold at arm's length, and sins inside it you have learned not to see? Ask who, in your own church, you should gently warn, and who outside it you should simply love.
